title: Python Basics
description: Learn the world's most versatile programming language. Python is the backbone of data science, AI, and automation.

lessons.title: Variables & Data Types
lessons.explanationHtml:
Python is dynamically typed, meaning you don't have to declare a variable's type (like integer or string) before using it. Python figures it out for you.

However, understanding the basic types—int, float, str (string), and bool (boolean)—is critical because you cannot perform mathematical operations on strings.

Recommended Resource

Python for Beginners - Programming with Mosh
lessons.codeExample:
age = 25          # int
price = 19.99     # float
name = "Alice"    # str
is_active = True  # bool

# String interpolation (f-strings)
print(f"Hello, my name is {name} and I am {age} years old.")

lessons.title: Lists & Dictionaries
lessons.explanationHtml:
When you need to store multiple items, you use Lists (arrays) and Dictionaries (hash maps/objects).

Lists are ordered and indexed by numbers, starting at 0. Dictionaries are unordered and indexed by "keys" (usually strings). Dictionaries are incredibly fast for looking up data.
lessons.codeExample:
# List
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
fruits.append("orange")
print(fruits[0]) # prints "apple"

# Dictionary
user = {
    "name": "Alice",
    "role": "Admin"
}
print(user["name"]) # prints "Alice"

lessons.title: Control Flow (If/Else & Loops)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Code reads top to bottom, but control flow allows you to skip lines or repeat them. Python uses indentation (spaces/tabs) to define code blocks instead of curly braces {}.

Use if/elif/else for logic, for loops to iterate over collections, and while loops to repeat until a condition is met.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.explanationHtml:
Functions allow you to encapsulate a block of code and reuse it simply by calling its name. This keeps your code DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself).

You define a function using the def keyword. Functions can take arguments (inputs) and return a value (output).
lessons.codeExample:
def calculate_tax(amount, tax_rate=0.2):
    """Calculates tax. Default rate is 20%."""
    return amount * tax_rate

tax = calculate_tax(100)
print(f"Tax is: ${tax}")

lessons.title: List Comprehensions
lessons.explanationHtml:
List comprehensions are a "Pythonic" way to create a new list by transforming an existing one in a single line of code.

They are significantly faster and cleaner than writing a standard for loop with an append() statement.
lessons.codeExample:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

# Traditional way
squares = []
for n in numbers:
    squares.append(n * n)

# List Comprehension
squares_fast = [n * n for n in numbers]

# With a condition
evens = [n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]

lessons.title: Classes & OOP
lessons.explanationHtml:
Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) allows you to bundle data and functions together into a single "Object". You create an object by first defining a blueprint called a class.

The __init__ method is the constructor, called automatically when you create a new instance of the class. The self keyword refers to the specific instance being manipulated.

lessons.title: Error Handling (Try/Except)
lessons.explanationHtml:
When Python encounters an error (like dividing by zero or reading a file that doesn't exist), it throws an Exception and crashes the program.

You can "catch" these exceptions using a try / except block, allowing your program to recover gracefully or log the error without shutting down.

lessons.title: File Handling (Context Managers)
lessons.explanationHtml:
When opening files in Python, you must remember to close them to free up system resources. If your code crashes before the close() method is called, the file remains locked.

The with statement (a Context Manager) automatically handles opening and securely closing the file for you, even if an exception occurs.
lessons.codeExample:
# Writing to a file
with open("data.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("Hello, File System!")

# Reading from a file
with open("data.txt", "r") as file:
    content = file.read()
    print(content)

title: SQL Fundamentals
description: Data is useless if you can't access it. Learn how to query relational databases, join tables, and extract actionable business insights.

lessons.title: SELECT & WHERE
lessons.explanationHtml:
SQL (Structured Query Language) is how you talk to relational databases like PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite. You extract data using the SELECT statement.

You almost never want to download an entire table. The WHERE clause allows you to filter rows on the database server before they are sent to your application.

Recommended Resource

SQL Tutorial - Full Database Course for Beginners (freeCodeCamp)
lessons.codeExample:
-- Get all columns
SELECT * FROM Users;

-- Get specific columns with filtering
SELECT first_name, email 
FROM Users 
WHERE age >= 18 
  AND status = 'active';

lessons.title: ORDER BY & LIMIT
lessons.explanationHtml:
Databases return rows in an unpredictable order by default. If you need a sorted list, you MUST use ORDER BY.

When building applications, you rarely show all records on one page. LIMIT combined with OFFSET allows you to implement pagination.
lessons.codeExample:
SELECT title, price 
FROM Products 
WHERE category = 'Electronics' 
ORDER BY price DESC 
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20; -- Shows results 21 to 30

lessons.title: Aggregate Functions
lessons.explanationHtml: SQL can perform calculations on your data instantly. Functions like COUNT(), SUM(), AVG(), MIN(), and MAX() allow you to summarize thousands of rows into a single value.

lessons.title: GROUP BY
lessons.explanationHtml:
Aggregate functions are powerful, but what if you want the average price per category? That's where GROUP BY comes in.

It groups rows that have the same values into summary rows. It is essential for data analytics and building dashboards.
lessons.codeExample:
SELECT category, COUNT(*) as product_count, AVG(price) as average_price
FROM Products
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY product_count DESC;

lessons.title: INNER JOIN
lessons.explanationHtml:
In a relational database, data is split across multiple tables to prevent duplication (Normalization). For example, Users and Orders.

To view an order alongside the user's email address, you must JOIN the tables together using a common key (usually an ID).
lessons.codeExample:
SELECT Orders.id, Orders.total, Users.email
FROM Orders
INNER JOIN Users ON Orders.user_id = Users.id
WHERE Orders.status = 'shipped';

lessons.title: LEFT & RIGHT JOINs
lessons.explanationHtml:
An INNER JOIN only returns rows if there is a match in BOTH tables. If a User hasn't made an Order, they disappear from the result.

A LEFT JOIN returns ALL rows from the left table (Users), and the matched rows from the right table (Orders). If there is no match, the right side will just contain NULL values.
lessons.codeExample:
SELECT Users.email, Orders.id
FROM Users
LEFT JOIN Orders ON Users.id = Orders.user_id;
-- Users with no orders will have a NULL Order ID

lessons.title: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
lessons.explanationHtml:
Querying data is safe, but modifying data is dangerous. You use INSERT INTO to create rows, UPDATE to modify them, and DELETE to remove them.

CRITICAL RULE: Never write an UPDATE or DELETE statement without a WHERE clause, or you will modify/delete every single row in the table.

lessons.title: Indexes for Performance
lessons.explanationHtml:
If you search a book for a specific word, you don't read every page; you use the index at the back. Databases work the same way.

If a table has millions of rows, querying WHERE email = '...' will cause a slow "Sequential Scan". Creating an index on the email column makes the lookup instantaneous, at the cost of slightly slower INSERTs.

title: LLM Engineering
description: Learn how to build AI-powered applications. Master prompt engineering, RAG, and interacting with the OpenAI API.

lessons.title: What is an LLM?
lessons.explanationHtml:
Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4 are essentially massive autocomplete engines. They don't "think" or "understand"; they predict the next most likely token (word fragment) based on the context window (your prompt).

Understanding this helps you write better prompts: you aren't asking a human a question, you are setting up a pattern for a machine to complete.

Recommended Resource

Let's build GPT: from scratch - Andrej Karpathy

lessons.title: Using the OpenAI API
lessons.explanationHtml:
To build an AI app, you interact with the model via a REST API. The OpenAI SDK makes this incredibly simple in Node.js or Python.

The chat completions endpoint accepts an array of messages. Messages have roles: system (instructions), user (the user's prompt), and assistant (the AI's previous replies).

lessons.title: Prompt Engineering Basics
lessons.explanationHtml:
Vague prompts yield bad answers. Good prompt engineering involves providing clear context, defining the desired output format, and using Few-Shot Learning (providing examples).

Adding "Let's think step by step" to a prompt forces the model to output its reasoning before answering, which drastically reduces logic errors (Chain of Thought reasoning).

lessons.title: Structured JSON Outputs
lessons.explanationHtml:
If you are integrating an LLM into software, you need it to return predictable data structures (like JSON) so your code can parse it. If it returns conversational text, your app will crash.

Modern APIs allow you to use "Function Calling" or "JSON Mode" to strictly enforce the shape of the output.

lessons.title: Vector Embeddings
lessons.explanationHtml:
Models don't understand text; they understand numbers. An embedding is a translation of text into an array of floating-point numbers (a vector).

Texts with similar meanings will have vectors that point in similar directions in multi-dimensional space. This allows you to perform "semantic search" (finding concepts that mean the same thing, even if they don't share exact keywords).

lessons.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
lessons.explanationHtml:
LLMs are frozen in time and don't know your company's private data. RAG solves this.

Instead of fine-tuning a model (which is expensive and hard to update), you: 1) Convert your private documents into embeddings. 2) When a user asks a question, search for the most relevant documents. 3) Inject those documents into the LLM prompt and ask it to answer the question using ONLY the provided context.

lessons.title: Streaming Responses
lessons.explanationHtml:
LLMs are slow. If it takes 5 seconds to generate a full paragraph, the user will stare at a loading spinner and think the app is broken.

By enabling stream: true, the API sends chunks of text as soon as they are generated (like ChatGPT typing). This dramatically improves the perceived performance of your application.
